title: How The Mona Lisa Was Stolen In A Broom Closet
sources: Louvre Museum Archives / Vanity Fair - On August 21, 1911, former Louvre glazier Vincenzo Peruggia hid overnight in a broom closet and carried out Leonardo's Mona Lisa.
The New York Times (1911-1913) - The painting was not noticed missing for 24 hours. The public hysteria turned the Mona Lisa into the most famous artwork in the world.

lines.text: Before nineteen eleven, the Mona Lisa was barely famous at all -

lines.text: until one museum worker hid in a broom closet overnight and stole it.
Vincenzo Peruggia was an Italian handyman working at the Louvre in Paris.
On a quiet Sunday evening, he slipped into a tiny maintenance closet and stayed there until morning.
When the museum was closed, he casually unhooked Leonardo da Vinci's masterpiece from the wall.
In a hidden stairwell, he stripped off the heavy glass frame and tucked the wooden panel under his white work smock.
He walked straight out the front gate and took the Mona Lisa home in a wooden trunk.
For twenty-four hours, not a single guard noticed the blank wall.
When the news broke, thousands of people lined up just to stare at the empty nail.
Front-page headlines turned the obscure painting into the most famous artwork on Earth.
Peruggia kept it under his bed for two years before finally getting caught trying to sell it.
The theft made Leonardo's portrait an overnight worldwide legend.
